The family was moving flats that month, and the house was all boxes, drilling and shouting. At first nobody noticed much about Noor, ten.
But Bhavna Masi, staying to help pack, did. Noor snapped at her little cousin over nothing. She lay on the sofa after school instead of going down to play cricket, which she used to beg for. She said her tummy hurt most mornings and cried when her pencil broke.
"She's just cranky from the move," Noor's father said, carrying a box.
"It's been three weeks," Masi said quietly. "She's stopped drawing too."
That night Masi sat on Noor's bed. "You seem heavy lately. Like a rain cloud." Noor's lip shook. "I don't know. I just don't want to do anything."
The next morning Masi and Noor's parents sat down together and booked a visit to the family doctor.

qa.q: What did Noor used to beg to go and do?
qa.a: Play cricket downstairs.

qa.q: How was Noor feeling underneath the crankiness?
qa.a: She seemed sad and low but couldn't say so, which came out as snapping, tiredness, tears and tummy aches.

qa.q: What did Bhavna Masi do well?
qa.a: She noticed that the change had lasted weeks, gently asked Noor about it and got the parents to book a doctor's visit instead of blaming the move.

qa.q: How might Noor's father have seen things before Masi spoke up?
qa.a: He was busy and stressed with the move and saw Noor as simply cranky, not as a child who was quietly struggling.

grounding: Noor seems cranky, tired and tearful, stops playing and has aches, and her aunt treats the lasting change as something that deserves attention.

passage:
In the village near Thrissur, Francis used to be first on the football ground after school. Now he came home and lay on his mat, scrolling his phone until two, then sleeping until noon on Sundays.
"He's become lazy," his father told the neighbour. "Attitude."
His sister Afreen noticed more. He hadn't answered his friends' calls in weeks. When she asked about football, he shrugged. "What's the point? I'm useless at everything anyway." His voice was flat, like it didn't belong to him.
That night Afreen sat with their parents. "It's not laziness. He's not himself. I think he needs a doctor."
Their mother was quiet, then nodded. On Monday she took Francis to the health centre, and the doctor referred him to a counsellor in town. Francis didn't say much, but he went.

qa.q: Where did Francis's mother take him on Monday?
qa.a: To the health centre.

qa.q: How does Francis seem to feel when he says he's useless at everything?
qa.a: He seems numb and worthless, speaking in a flat voice and pulling away from things he used to enjoy.

qa.q: What went wrong in how Francis's father saw things, and what fixed it?
qa.a: He called it laziness and attitude; Afreen named it as a health matter, and the family got him to a doctor and a counsellor.

qa.q: How might Afreen feel watching her brother change?
qa.a: She is probably worried and sad, missing the brother who was first on the football ground.

grounding: Francis sleeps and scrolls for hours, drops friends and football and feels worthless, and his sister sees it as a health matter needing a doctor, not laziness.

passage:
You asked how it was with Darshan last year. I'm Manoj, his father, and I'll be honest, I got it wrong at first.
He was fifteen. He stopped eating dinner with us, stayed in his room, snapped when I asked anything. One night I lost my temper. "What is wrong with you? Just cheer up, you have everything!" He slammed the door.
I sat in the hall feeling useless and angry, mostly at myself.
The next morning I knocked, sat on the edge of his bed and said, "I'm sorry for shouting. I'm worried about you. You don't have to explain everything. I'm just here." He didn't speak for a long time. Then he said, "I feel heavy all the time, Papa."
That week, we saw the school counsellor, and she helped us find a psychologist. He's better now. Slowly. I learned to listen first.

qa.q: What did Manoj shout at Darshan that night?
qa.a: "What is wrong with you? Just cheer up, you have everything!"

qa.q: How did Manoj feel sitting in the hall after the door slammed?
qa.a: He felt useless and angry, mostly at himself.

qa.q: What changed in Manoj's approach, and why did it help?
qa.a: He apologised, showed concern instead of blame, listened without demanding answers and arranged professional support, which let Darshan open up.

qa.q: What was it like for Darshan to hear "Just cheer up"?
qa.a: He probably felt misunderstood and more alone, as if his heavy feeling was his fault.

grounding: Manoj sees his son pull away and snap, feels helpless and angry, and learns that concern, listening and professional support help more than telling him to cheer up.

subtype: Heavy days behind a functioning face [Actor]
passage:
"You came to every lecture this week, Saurabh. Top marks in the quiz, too," Kamal said, as they sat on the hostel steps at four o'clock.
"Yeah. I come. I sit. I go back to the room and lie there."
"You look exhausted."
"I am. Everything feels empty. Honestly, sometimes I think everyone would be happier if I just wasn't here."
Kamal went still. He turned to face Saurabh. "I'm really glad you told me. I need to ask you straight. Are you thinking of ending your life?"
"I don't know. I think about it."
"Okay. Thank you for being honest. I'm not leaving you. The counselling centre is open right now. Will you walk there with me?"
Saurabh stared at the ground. "What if they think I'm dramatic?"
"They won't. And I'll sit with you the whole time."
Saurabh nodded. Kamal stood up and held out his hand, and they walked over together.

qa.q: Where were Saurabh and Kamal sitting?
qa.a: On the hostel steps at four o'clock.

qa.q: How was Saurabh feeling behind his good attendance and marks?
qa.a: He felt empty, exhausted and hopeless, even thinking everyone would be happier if he wasn't there.

qa.q: Why was Kamal's response the right one?
qa.a: He took the words seriously, asked directly, stayed with Saurabh and went with him to the counselling centre right away instead of leaving it for later.

qa.q: How might Kamal be feeling as he asks the direct question?
qa.a: He is probably frightened and shaken, but he stays calm because he cares and wants Saurabh safe.

grounding: Saurabh keeps attending class but feels empty and hopeless and thinks others would be better off without him, and his friend responds at once and takes him to get help.

passage:
Alka had been annoyed with Tarun for weeks. He had cancelled their Sunday walk to the temple tank twice, skipped her sister's engagement, and stopped answering in the group chat. In the college canteen in Sangli, he pushed his plate away again.
When she joked, "Coming to the fair on Friday?" he muttered, "What's the point. Nothing's going to get better anyway."
The words stayed with her. That evening she went to his house and asked him to sit with her on the steps, away from the others. "You haven't been eating, and what you said today scared me. Are you thinking of hurting yourself?"
He looked at his hands. "No. I'm just so tired of everything."
Alka stayed. She listened for a long time. Before she left, with his okay, they told his elder sister together, and his sister booked the college counsellor for the next morning. Alka texted him before bed: "I'm here."

qa.q: What did Tarun mutter when Alka asked about the fair?
qa.a: "What's the point. Nothing's going to get better anyway."

qa.q: How did Alka's feelings change after Tarun's remark?
qa.a: Her annoyance at the cancelled plans turned into worry and fear for him; the words stayed with her.

qa.q: What did Alka do that showed real care?
qa.a: She checked in privately that same evening, asked directly, listened and stayed, involved his sister and encouraged the counsellor visit, then texted before bed.

qa.q: How might Tarun feel when Alka turns up at his house?
qa.a: He might feel exposed at first, then less alone and cared for because she came to him rather than giving up.

grounding: Alka notices Tarun's missed meals, cancelled plans and dark remark, checks in privately, listens and stays, and gently gets him professional help.

Warden's note, girls' hostel, Block C.
Over the last two weeks I have seen Charu, from Room 14, quietly looking after her roommate Preeti, who has been missing classes and meals and staying in bed.
Charu doesn't lecture her or tell her to smile. Each evening she says, "Walk to the gate and back?" Some days Preeti says no. Some days she goes. On Sunday they cooked instant noodles together in the pantry and ate on the floor.
Yesterday Charu came to my office. "I helped her book an appointment with the campus doctor for Thursday. But I'm getting tired, and last night she said something that worried me." We spoke to Preeti together, and with her agreement I called her mother the same evening. Charu has also agreed to take a break this weekend with her own friends.

qa.q: Where did Charu and Preeti eat the noodles they cooked?
qa.a: On the floor, after cooking them together in the pantry.

qa.q: How was Charu feeling when she came to the warden's office?
qa.a: She felt tired and anxious, worn down from caring and worried by something Preeti had said.

qa.q: What did Charu get right as a supporter?
qa.a: She offered small, doable things like walks and shared meals, didn't demand cheerfulness, helped book the doctor, respected her own limits and brought in the warden and family when worried about safety.

qa.q: What might Preeti feel about Charu's quiet support?
qa.a: Preeti may feel trust and some comfort, since Charu stays close without pressuring her to be cheerful.

grounding: A warden notes how Charu supports her low roommate with small actions and a doctor's appointment, looks after her own limits and involves others when worried about safety.

passage:
Payal had loved her job at the cooperative bank in Satara. Now she sat at the counter and felt nothing. Her favourite music, Sunday lunches at her parents', even the new saree her husband Imran bought her, all felt grey.
At home, she stared at the washing for an hour, unable to start. Then she lay awake feeling guilty. "Imran does everything. I'm a burden," she thought. "This is just who I am now."
One morning Imran found her sitting on the kitchen floor, not crying, just blank. He sat beside her. "This isn't you being lazy. This is something that needs a doctor."
At the district hospital, the doctor listened and made a plan with her, including regular sessions with a counsellor. "What you're feeling tells you it will last forever," the doctor said. "It usually doesn't, with help." Payal held on to that sentence.

qa.q: Where did Payal work?
qa.a: At the cooperative bank in Satara.

qa.q: How did Payal feel lying awake at night?
qa.a: She felt guilty and like a burden, and hopeless, believing this was just who she was now.

qa.q: What helped Payal start moving towards feeling better?
qa.a: Imran's supportive words that it wasn't laziness, and seeing a doctor who made a treatment plan with counselling.

qa.q: How does Imran see Payal's struggle?
qa.a: He sees it as a health problem that needs a doctor, not a character flaw, and feels caring and concerned.

grounding: Payal stops enjoying anything, can't start tasks and feels guilty, and a supportive husband and qualified doctor help her see it need not be permanent.

passage:
On a crowded tram in Gothenburg, Anders was scrolling through a football video when his heart began to pound. The carriage seemed to tilt. His hands tingled, and a thought rushed in: something terrible is happening.
He grabbed the pole. His friend Lucia said, "Anders? You've gone white."
"I think I'm dying," he whispered.
He got off at the next stop and sat on a bench, gulping air. Slowly, the pounding eased. The world stopped tilting. It passed.
But the next morning he told his mum he'd walk the long way to school. And the next. By Friday he'd stopped going to the shopping centre with friends too, just in case. Lucia noticed. "You can't walk everywhere forever," she said gently. "Tell your mum what really happened."

qa.q: What was Anders watching when his heart began to pound?
qa.a: A football video.

qa.q: What was Anders feeling on the tram?
qa.a: He felt terrified, with a pounding heart, dizziness and a sense that something terrible was happening, even that he was dying.

qa.q: What went wrong after the attack, and what small step does Lucia suggest?
qa.a: His fear of another one made him avoid the tram and the shopping centre; Lucia suggests telling his mum what really happened so he can get help.

qa.q: How does Lucia see Anders's new habit of walking everywhere?
qa.a: She notices and feels concerned that his life is getting smaller, and wants him to get support.

grounding: Anders has a sudden wave of fear with a pounding heart and dizziness that passes, but fear of the next one begins to shrink his life.

passage:
In the changing room at the swimming club in Lisbon, Oskar suddenly sat down hard on the bench. His breath came fast and shallow. "I can't breathe. Something's wrong."
Layla didn't crowd him or call everyone over. She crouched a little distance away and spoke slowly. "I'm right here, Oskar. This is a wave. It feels awful, and it will pass."
"It won't," he gasped.
She didn't argue. "Okay. Just feel your feet on the floor. Breathe out slowly with me." She breathed out, long and steady. He tried to copy her.
Gradually his shoulders dropped. He wiped his face.
Walking home, Layla said, "Has this happened before?"
"Twice."
"Then will you tell your dad tonight and see the doctor? Or the school counsellor? You shouldn't carry it alone." Oskar nodded, and she walked him to his door.

qa.q: Where was Oskar when the attack started?
qa.a: In the changing room at the swimming club.

qa.q: How was Oskar feeling when he sat down hard on the bench?
qa.a: He was frightened and panicky, breathing fast and sure something was wrong.

qa.q: Which of Layla's choices helped most, and why?
qa.a: Staying close without crowding, speaking slowly, saying it would pass without arguing, then urging a doctor or counsellor because it had happened before.

qa.q: What is it like for Oskar to have Layla there?
qa.a: He likely feels less alone and a bit calmer, able to copy her steady breathing instead of being swept away by fear.

grounding: Layla stays close, speaks slowly and reminds Oskar the panic will pass without arguing or crowding, then encourages him to see a doctor or counsellor since it has recurred.

passage:
"Jomon, the exam hall is that way."
"I know, Leela. I'm taking it in the small room. I told the office I have a headache."
"You did that last month too. And you stopped taking the metro."
Jomon sighed. "Because of what happened in March. What if it happens in the hall? Two hundred people watching me."
"The panic thing?"
"Yes. My heart went crazy, I couldn't breathe, I thought I was dying. Now I'm scared all the time of it coming back."
"That sounds exhausting. Did you ever find out what it was?"
"No."
"My cousin had the same. The counsellor explained it's the body's alarm going off when there's no fire. Knowing that helped her a lot. Come with me to the student wellness centre after this?"
Jomon was quiet. "If I understood it, maybe I wouldn't be so scared of it."
"Exactly. After the exam, then."

qa.q: How many people did Jomon imagine watching in the exam hall?
qa.a: Two hundred people.

qa.q: Why did Jomon ask for the small room?
qa.a: He felt scared that panic would strike again in front of everyone, so he was avoiding the big hall.

qa.q: What does Leela suggest, and why could it help?
qa.a: Going to the student wellness centre, because understanding the body's alarm and getting professional guidance can reduce the fear.

qa.q: How might Leela feel watching Jomon avoid things?
qa.a: She seems concerned and caring, noticing the pattern and wanting him to get help rather than keep hiding.

grounding: Jomon avoids exam halls and the metro in case panic strikes again, and a friend points him toward understanding his body's alarm and professional guidance.
